name: Gene Editing Guide Design
title: Gene Editing Guide Design
answer: Gene editing guide design is the computational task of choosing short RNA sequences that direct a CRISPR-associated nuclease to a target DNA site while minimizing off-target cleavage and maximizing on-target efficiency. It spans single guide RNA selection for Cas9, Cas12, base editors, and prime editors, and includes scoring candidate guides against reference genomes, transcriptomes, and patient-specific variants. The work sits inside genomic medicine because a poorly chosen guide can cause unintended edits, failed repair outcomes, or safety problems in therapeutic cells. It is not the same as designing the repair template or measuring the edit after delivery, though those steps depend on the guide.

sections.body: Gene editing guide design is the computational task of choosing short RNA sequences that direct a CRISPR-associated nuclease to a target DNA site while minimizing off-target cleavage and maximizing on-target efficiency. It spans single guide RNA selection for Cas9, Cas12, base editors, and prime editors, and includes scoring candidate guides against reference genomes, transcriptomes, and patient-specific variants. The work sits inside genomic medicine because a poorly chosen guide can cause unintended edits, failed repair outcomes, or safety problems in therapeutic cells. It is not the same as designing the repair template or measuring the edit after delivery, though those steps depend on the guide.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Guide design runs on standard bioinformatics infrastructure: reference genome builds, variant call files, and annotation databases for genes, regulatory elements, and known off-target sites. Most tools are deployed as command-line programs, web portals, or cloud pipelines that accept a target region or gene and return ranked guide sequences. Compute needs are modest compared with large language model training, often a single CPU or GPU per design job, but whole-genome off-target search can require indexed alignment or k-mer matching across billions of positions. The site's tracking of 732 AI tools and 803 scientific models reflects the broader ecosystem in which these design tools are catalogued, though the guide design tools themselves are usually specialized bioinformatics packages rather than general medical AI models.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by scoring candidate guides with a mix of empirical rules and learned models. Classical methods use position-specific nucleotide preferences, GC content, melting temperature, and mismatch counts against potential off-target sites. Modern approaches train gradient-boosted trees or convolutional neural networks on large libraries of measured on-target and off-target editing outcomes, then use those models to rank guides for a new target. Some pipelines also incorporate structural or epigenetic features, such as chromatin accessibility or DNA methylation, when those data are available for the cell type of interest. The output is typically a ranked list with scores for efficiency, specificity, and predicted repair outcome, not a single guaranteed best guide.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in guide design center on patient safety, data provenance, and liability for unintended edits. A guide that looks specific in a reference genome may still cut a rare variant in a patient, so clinical use requires re-scoring against the patient's own sequence and documenting the source and version of every genome build, annotation, and model. Product liability and wrongful death claims against AI companies, tracked on this site, are a reminder that design software can become part of a therapeutic workflow where an error has serious consequences. Compliance and regulation pages cover how guide design tools are validated, how off-target evidence is reported to regulators, and how informed consent describes the limits of computational prediction. No design tool removes the need for empirical testing in the actual edited cell type.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where guide design is going is toward models that predict not just where a nuclease cuts but the full editing outcome, including indel patterns, base conversion, and unintended large deletions or chromosomal rearrangements. The field is also moving from reference-genome scoring to personal genome scoring, where a guide is re-ranked against a patient's variants before any therapeutic edit. As more editing outcomes are measured at scale, learned models are likely to improve on the current reliance on small, biased training sets. In the longer term, guide design may merge with repair template design and delivery vector choice into a single planning step for a genetic medicine.
